title: He Had $70,000 and the Smithsonian. Two Bicycle Mechanics Beat Him in 9 Days.
description: In 1903, Samuel Langley had government money, the Smithsonian, and the best engineers in America. Two bicycle mechanics from Ohio had almost nothing. This is how Wilbur and Orville Wright beat him to the first airplane flight, and the bitter fight over who deserved the credit.
notes: FACT-CHECK before recording: NYT editorial Oct 9, 1903 ('one million to ten million years'); Langley funding (~$50,000 War Dept + Smithsonian funds, ~$70,000 total is a common estimate); Wrights' budget 'under $1,000' (their own account); Oct 7 and Dec 8, 1903 Aerodrome failures; Dec 17 flight times/distances (12s/120ft, 59s/852ft); five witnesses; Charlie Taylor engine; wind tunnel Fall 1901, ~200 wing shapes; Langley died Feb 1906; 1914 Curtiss Aerodrome flights; Smithsonian label until 1928; Flyer to London 1928, returned Dec 1948.

scenes.text: On October ninth, nineteen oh three, the New York Times published a prediction. A flying machine, it said, might be developed in a million to ten million years. Ten weeks later, two bicycle mechanics from Ohio proved the newspaper wrong. And the man the paper was mocking had been given about seventy thousand dollars, mostly of public money, to do it first.

Samuel Pierpont Langley was the obvious favourite. Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution. A celebrated astronomer. Friends in Washington, a team of engineers, and the backing of the War Department. If anyone in America was going to fly, everyone assumed it would be him.

Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. Neither had a college degree. By their own account, they spent less than a thousand dollars on their first airplane, mostly from the money the shop made.

But they had something Langley didn't: a different question. Langley believed flight was a power problem. Build a strong enough engine, a big enough wing, and the machine would rise. The Wrights thought the real problem was control. A bird doesn't just float. It steers, constantly. And a bicycle had taught them that something unstable can be balanced, if the rider adjusts it every second.

Then they hit a wall. The published data on wing lift, from the famous glider pioneer Otto Lilienthal, turned out to be wrong. Their gliders performed worse than predicted. So in the autumn of nineteen oh one, they built something no one in their business had ever needed. A wind tunnel. A wooden box with a fan.
They tested over two hundred wing shapes. It cost almost nothing, and it gave them the best aerodynamic data in the world. The brothers weren't guessing anymore.
scenes.image: Wright brothers wind tunnel wing models

scenes.text: No engine maker could supply a motor light enough. So their shop mechanic, Charlie Taylor, built one in about six weeks. And the brothers designed their propellers as rotating wings, a problem no one had solved properly before.

Meanwhile, Langley's machine, the Great Aerodrome, was a feat of engineering muscle. It was launched from the roof of a houseboat on the Potomac River, with a pilot named Charles Manly. But it gave the pilot very little control once it was in the air.

On October seventh, nineteen oh three, it was launched. The machine caught on the launch rail and plunged straight into the river. Manly was pulled out, shaken but alive. Two days later, the Times wrote its million-year prediction.

Langley had one more try. On December eighth, he launched again. This time the tail tore away, and the aerodrome fell into the Potomac once more. The government's money was gone. So was his reputation.

Nine days later, on a windswept strip of sand at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright lay down on the lower wing of the Wright Flyer. At ten thirty-five that morning, it lifted off the track. Twelve seconds. A hundred and twenty feet. Shorter than the wingspan of a jumbo jet.

They flew four times that day. The last flight, with Wilbur at the controls, lasted fifty-nine seconds and covered eight hundred and fifty-two feet. For the first time, a human being had flown in a powered, controlled airplane. Only five people saw it happen.

And the world barely noticed. Newspapers called the claim exaggerated. Many simply didn't believe it. The brothers returned to Ohio, and kept improving their machine in a quiet field outside Dayton, with almost no audience.
Langley died in nineteen oh six, after years of ridicule. But the story has one more cruel turn.

In a patent fight years later, a rival rebuilt Langley's aerodrome with major changes, and flew it. And the Smithsonian displayed that machine for years with a label calling it the first aeroplane in the history of the world capable of carrying a man in sustained free flight.
Orville was furious. In protest, he sent the original Wright Flyer, the machine that made history, to a museum in London. Not to Washington. To another country.
It stayed there for twenty years. Orville died in nineteen forty-eight. And the Wright Flyer finally came home to the Smithsonian that same year, where it hangs to this day.
scenes.image: Wright Flyer National Air and Space Museum

scenes.text: Langley had money, talent, and power. The Wrights had a question nobody else was asking. Not how do we leave the ground? But how do we stay in control once we're up there?
A million to ten million years. That was the prediction. It took ten weeks.
